Informed\n\nDocs npmversion github Docs\n\n## Introduction\n\nSay hello to the best React form library you have ever used! Informed is an extensive, simple, and efficient solution for creating basic to complex forms in React. Out of the box you get the ability to grab and manipulate values, validate fields, create custom inputs, multi-step forms, array fields, and much much more!\n\nOh and YES WE USE HOOKS!\n\n## Getting Started\n\n##### Install with npm\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install --save informed\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n#### Live Examples / Docs\n\nDocs Docs\n\n### What Can it do ?\n\nSee for yourself.\n\nBy default it comes with native dom inputs that are controlled by informed.\n\nimport { Form, Input, Select, Checkbox, Relevant, Debug } from 'informed';\n\nconst onSubmit = ({ values }) =\u003e console.log(values);\n\nconst ExampleForm = () =\u003e (\n  \u003cForm onSubmit={onSubmit}\u003e\n    \u003cInput name=\"name\" label=\"Name\" placeholder=\"Elon\" /\u003e\n    \u003cInput name=\"age\" type=\"number\" label=\"Age\" required=\"Age Required\" /\u003e\n    \u003cInput name=\"phone\" label=\"Phone\" formatter=\"+1 (###)-###-####\" /\u003e\n    \u003cSelect name=\"car\" label=\"Car\" initialValue=\"ms\"\u003e\n      \u003coption value=\"ms\"\u003eModel S\u003c/option\u003e\n      \u003coption value=\"m3\"\u003eModel 3\u003c/option\u003e\n      \u003coption value=\"mx\"\u003eModel X\u003c/option\u003e\n      \u003coption value=\"my\"\u003eModel Y\u003c/option\u003e\n    \u003c/Select\u003e\n    \u003cCheckbox name=\"married\" label=\"Married?\" /\u003e\n    \u003cRelevant when={({ formState }) =\u003e formState.values.married}\u003e\n      \u003cInput name=\"spouse\" label=\"Spouse\" /\u003e\n    \u003c/Relevant\u003e\n    \u003cbutton type=\"submit\"\u003eSubmit\u003c/button\u003e\n    \u003cDebug /\u003e\n  \u003c/Form\u003e\n);\n\n## Feature List\n\n&#96;informed&#96; was designed to support many important features\n\n* Arrays: ability to render dynamic arrays of fields &#96;[ 'a', 'b' ]&#96; or &#96;[ { name: 'Joe', age: 29 }, { name: 'Hope', age: 24 }]&#96;\n* Relevance: ability to render render fields conditionally depending on the state of other parts of the form\n* JSPAN: ability to easily and intuitively manipulate form state\n* Formatting: ability to perform display formatting, where the format shown to user can differ from the state of the values stored\n* Validation: ability to perform both synchronous and asynchronous validation in a controlled manner\n* Api: ability to manipulate the form state both inside and outside the context of the form\n* State: ability to access field and form data\n* Multistep: ability to create dynamic multistep forms\n* Scope: ability to scope ( group ) fields\n* Schema: ability to render forms based on pure JSON schema\n* Dynaic: ability to hide and show fields ( render and unrender ) and either cleanup or maintain state of unmounted fields\n* Debugging: ability to easily debug user's state as well as internals of the library\n* Nesting: ability to have highly nested value structure &#96;state.values.friends[1].brother.parents.cars[0].model&#96;\n\n## Creating Your Own Fields\n\nBut what if you dont want the out of the box stuff??\n\nNo problem, see example below!\n\nimport { useForm, useField, Relevant, FormState } from 'informed';\n\n// Step 1. Build your form component ---------------------\n\nconst Form = ({ children, ...rest }) =\u003e {\n  const { formController, render, userProps } = useForm(rest);\n\n  return render(\n    \u003cform noValidate {...userProps} onSubmit={formController.submitForm}\u003e\n      {children}\n    \u003c/form\u003e\n  );\n};\n\n// Step 2. Build your input components --------------------\n\nconst Input = props =\u003e {\n  const { render, informed, userProps, ref } = useField({\n    type: 'text',\n    ...props\n  });\n  const { label, id, ...rest } = userProps;\n  return render(\n    \u003c\u003e\n      \u003clabel htmlFor={id}\u003e{label}\u003c/label\u003e\n      \u003cinput id={id} ref={ref} {...informed} {...rest} /\u003e\n    \u003c/\u003e\n  );\n};\n\nconst Checkbox = props =\u003e {\n  const { render, informed, userProps, ref } = useField({\n    type: 'checkbox',\n    ...props\n  });\n  const { label, id, ...rest } = userProps;\n  return render(\n    \u003c\u003e\n      \u003clabel htmlFor={id}\u003e{label}\u003c/label\u003e\n      \u003cinput id={id} ref={ref} {...informed} {...rest} /\u003e\n    \u003c/\u003e\n  );\n};\n\nconst ErrorInput = props =\u003e {\n  const { render, informed, userProps, fieldState, ref } = useField({\n    type: 'text',\n    ...props\n  });\n  const { label, id, ...rest } = userProps;\n  const { showError } = fieldState;\n  const style = showError ? { border: 'solid 1px red' } : null;\n  return render(\n    \u003c\u003e\n      \u003clabel htmlFor={id}\u003e{label}\u003c/label\u003e\n      \u003cinput id={id} ref={ref} {...informed} {...rest} style={style} /\u003e\n      {showError \u0026\u0026 \u003csmall style={{ color: 'red' }}\u003e{fieldState.error}\u003c/small\u003e}\n    \u003c/\u003e\n  );\n};\n\nconst Select = props =\u003e {\n  const { render, informed, userProps, ref } = useField({\n    type: 'select',\n    ...props\n  });\n  const { label, id, children, ...rest } = userProps;\n  return render(\n    \u003c\u003e\n      \u003clabel htmlFor={id}\u003e{label}\u003c/label\u003e\n      \u003cselect id={id} ref={ref} {...informed} {...rest}\u003e\n        {children}\n      \u003c/select\u003e\n    \u003c/\u003e\n  );\n};\n\n// Step 3. Build your forms! ---------------------------\n\nconst onSubmit = ({ values }) =\u003e console.log(values);\n\nconst ExampleForm = () =\u003e (\n  \u003cForm onSubmit={onSubmit}\u003e\n    \u003cInput name=\"name\" label=\"Name\" placeholder=\"Elon\" /\u003e\n    \u003cErrorInput name=\"age\" type=\"number\" label=\"Age\" required=\"Age Required\" /\u003e\n    \u003cInput name=\"phone\" label=\"Phone\" formatter=\"+1 (###)-###-####\" /\u003e\n    \u003cSelect name=\"car\" label=\"Car\" initialValue=\"ms\"\u003e\n      \u003coption value=\"ms\"\u003eModel S\u003c/option\u003e\n      \u003coption value=\"m3\"\u003eModel 3\u003c/option\u003e\n      \u003coption value=\"mx\"\u003eModel X\u003c/option\u003e\n      \u003coption value=\"my\"\u003eModel Y\u003c/option\u003e\n    \u003c/Select\u003e\n    \u003cCheckbox name=\"married\" label=\"Married?\" /\u003e\n    \u003cRelevant when={({ formState }) =\u003e formState.values.married}\u003e\n      \u003cInput name=\"spouse\" label=\"Spouse\" /\u003e\n    \u003c/Relevant\u003e\n    \u003cbutton type=\"submit\"\u003eSubmit\u003c/button\u003e\n    \u003cDebug /\u003e\n  \u003c/Form\u003e\n);\n\n---\n\n## For Contributors\n\n### Design\n\nInformed took the following into consideration when being built:\n\n* **Performance:** &#96;informed&#96; was designed to be able to handle very complex forms at scale  \n   * Ability to render a form with thousands of fields on screen  \n   * Ability to bulk update thousands of fields at a time\n* **Readability** &#96;informed&#96; was designed to be able to write complex forms with very little **intuitive** code  \n   * Reads naturally like with pure JSX:\n\n\u003cForm onSubmit={onSubmit}\u003e\n  \u003cInput name=\"name\" label=\"Name\" placeholder=\"Elon\" /\u003e\n  \u003cInput name=\"age\" type=\"number\" label=\"Age\" required=\"Age Required\" /\u003e\n  \u003cInput name=\"phone\" label=\"Phone\" formatter=\"+1 (###)-###-####\" /\u003e\n  \u003cCheckbox name=\"married\" label=\"Married?\" /\u003e\n  \u003cRelevant when={({ formState }) =\u003e formState.values.married}\u003e\n    \u003cInput name=\"spouse\" label=\"Spouse\" /\u003e\n  \u003c/Relevant\u003e\n  \u003cDebug /\u003e\n\u003c/Form\u003e\n\n* **ZERO Dependency:** &#96;informed&#96; was designed to rely on no other library  \n   * exception of a peer dependency react... for now ;)\n* **JSON Schema:** &#96;informed&#96; was designed to support rendering forms based on pure JSON  \n   * this is especially useful when form definitions are stored on the backend\n* **Feature List:** &#96;informed&#96; was designed to support many important features  \n   * Arrays: ability to render dynamic arrays of fields &#96;[ 'a', 'b' ]&#96; or &#96;[ { name: 'Joe', age: 29 }, { name: 'Hope', age: 24 }]&#96;  \n   * Relevance: ability to render render fields conditionally depending on the state of other parts of the form  \n   * JSPAN: ability to easily and intuitively manipulate form state  \n   * Formatting: ability to perform display formatting, where the format shown to user can differ from the state of the values stored  \n   * Validation: ability to perform both synchronous and asynchronous validation in a controlled manner  \n   * Api: ability to manipulate the form state both inside and outside the context of the form  \n   * State: ability to access field and form data  \n   * Multistep: ability to create dynamic multistep forms  \n   * Scope: ability to scope ( group ) fields  \n   * Schema: ability to render forms based on pure JSON schema  \n   * Dynaic: ability to hide and show fields ( render and unrender ) and either cleanup or maintain state of unmounted fields  \n   * Debugging: ability to easily debug user's state as well as internals of the library  \n   * Nesting: ability to have highly nested value strucutre &#96;state.values.friends[1].brother.parents.cars[0].model&#96;\n\n---\n\n### Terminology\n\n* **JSPAN:** ( Java Script Path Access Notation ) much like how you access and write to objects and arrays in javascript you can use the string representation to address a place in an object.\n\nconst path = 'state.values.friends[1].brother.name';\n\n---\n\n### Layout\n\nThis project cotains three important directories, &#96;src&#96;, &#96;vitedocs&#96;, and &#96;__tests__&#96;\n\n**Note:** some things were left out as they are not super important or are going to be deprecated or removed in future.\n\nproject_root\n│\n├── index.d.ts        # all of informeds types live here\n│\n├── src               # all of informeds source code lives here ( except types index.d.ts )\n│   ├── components        # React Components\n│   ├── hooks             # Hooks\n│   ├── Context.js        # Internal Contexts used in this library\n│   ├── debug.js          # Basically the https://github.com/visionmedia/debug library but shrunk down\n│   ├── fieldMap.js       # Default field adapter, used when working with schema forms\n│   ├── index.js          # all external exports ( everything exposed to users )\n│   ├── ObjectMap.js      # internal data structure for manipulating the form state objects\n│   ├── FormController.js # The brains behind the library, this controls basically everything :)\n│   └── utils.js          # Any utilities used throughout this project\n│\n├── vitedocs          # All the informed docs build via vite ( instead of storybook which was old way )\n│   ├── App.jsx           # basic react app with react-router\n│   ├── Header            # top nav of the docs\n│   ├── hooks             # helper hooks for docs\n│   ├── Nav               # side nav of the docs\n│   ├── Pages             # main level pages of the app\n│   │   ├──ApiReference       # Self explanatory :)\n│   │   ├──Examples           # Examples of all sorts of usecases\n│   │   ├──GettingStarted     # Also Self explanatory :)\n│   │   └──Playground.jsx     # Uses Sandpack to allow users to test any of the examples\n│   │\n│   ├── SideBySide.jsx    # helper component for showing code example and output side by side\n│   ├── index.css         # documentation styles\n│   ├── prism.css         # styles for code blocks\n│   └── ...               # other stuff\n│\n└── __tests__           # extensive unit testing\n    ├── components      # tests for informed components\n    ├── hooks           # tests for informed hooks\n    ├── ObjectMap.test  # tests for the internal data structure\n    ├── Schema.test     # tests for usage of JSON schema rendered forms\n    └── utils.test      # tests for internal library utilities\n\n---\n\n### Key Components\n\n#### &#96;FormController&#96;\n\nFormController is the brains of informed, it holds the &#96;state&#96; object and is responsible for:\n\n* Managing the form state\n* Tracking all form fields via registration/deregistration\n* Managing events. FormController implements its own event hand;er ( a few lines of code at bottom of file )\n\n#### &#96;ObjectMap&#96;\n\nObjectMap is the internal data structre that is responsible for managing the internal state object. Reads and writes all go through this data structure. Example:\n\n// State object\nconst state = { values: {} };\n\n// Set the states values first friends brothers age to 30\nObjectMap.set(state.values, 'friends[0].brothers.age', 30);\n\n#### &#96;useField&#96;\n\nuseField is the first class citizen of informed, it's responsible for registering a field by name to the FormController.\n\n#### Context\n\nThough there is not explicitly a component called &#96;Context&#96; here the concept is KEY to understanding informed. Context alows us to register fields in a highly nested structure and allows us to do wild things such as scoping.\n\n---\n\n### Architecture Diagram\n\nBelow depicts the core to how this library works. Form controller is the master of all form elements and everyone else just subscribes to events that it triggers. The events can be caused by function calls from elsewhere. In the example below we depict what happens when a user types in an \"H\" in the name field\n\n##### Code:\n\n\u003cForm\u003e\n  \u003cInput name=\"name\" /\u003e {/* --\u003e useField(\"name\") --\u003e useFieldState(\"name\") */}\n  \u003cDebug /\u003e {/* --\u003e useFormState() */}\n\u003c/Form\u003e\n\n##### Diagram: ( when user types the letter \"H\" )\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n     +----------------+\n     | FormController | \u003c ──────────────────────────────────────────\n     |   state {}     |                                             │\n     +-------+--------+                                             │\n             │                                                      │\n             │ event(\"field\", \"name\")                               │\n             v                                                      │\n    +-------------------+                                           │\n    |    Event System   | ────────────────                          │\n    +--------+----+-----+                 │                         │\n             │                            │                         │\n             │ event(\"field\", \"name\")     │ event(\"field\", \"name\")  │ setValue(\"H\")\n             │                            │                         │\n             v                            v                         │\n    +-------------------+       +------------------------+          │\n    |   useFormState()  |       |  useFieldState(\"name\") |          │\n    +-------------------+       +------------------------+          │\n             ^                            ^                         │\n             │ uses                       │ uses                    │\n             │                            │                         │\n    +-------------------+       +------------------------+          │\n    |      \u003cDebug /\u003e    |       |    useField(\"name\")    | ─────────\n    +-------------------+       +------------------------+\n                                          ^\n                                          │ uses\n                                          │\n                                +------------------------+\n                                | \u003cInput name=\"name\" /\u003e  |\n                                +------------------------+\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n---\n\n### Types ( Type Script )\n\nI know, I know the types kinda suck. I personally don't use typescript so I have had to rely on other TS wizard devs to help maintain the types. When trying to type very complex objects such as &#96;FormState&#96; especially parts like &#96;FormState.values&#96; which can literally be an object that contains anything there are lots of opinions on how to properly type it. I'm actively seeking help here.\n\n---\n\n### Documentation\n\nAs stated earlier, docs now live in the vitedocs directory. Its called &#96;vitedocs&#96; because I migrated them from storybook to now use a custom singe page react app built with &#96;vite&#96;... pronounced \"veet\" by the way :)\n\n#### What to expect\n\nMost of the docs contain examples where each example has a directory.\n\nFor example, if you look at the &#96;vitedocs/Pages/GettingStarted/CarColors&#96; you will find the &#96;CarColors.jsx&#96; file. This file contains the page that gets shown ( whatever info you want to show on that page ) and then the example itself.\n\nBecause we use vite, we can take advantage of the fact that vite can import both a react component normally, and also the raw text from that file! Therefore creating examples is as simple as this!\n\n**Note** how we make use of the &#96;SideBySide&#96; component to render our code and example\n\nimport Example from './Example';\nimport exampleCode from './Example.jsx?raw';\n\n//... other stuff\n\u003cSideBySide\n  leftHeader={\u003ch3\u003eExample: \u003c/h3\u003e}\n  rightHeader={\u003ch3\u003eCode:\u003c/h3\u003e}\n  left={\u003cExample /\u003e}\n  right={\u003cCode links input1={exampleCode} /\u003e}\n/\u003e;\n\n### TODO/Improvements\n\n* re-write the internal implementation of how schemas are rendered, that code is not my favorite\n* re-write the way multistep forms work. Currently they step through each step when navigating to a step only initializing the values for that step when its rendered\n* allow an evaluate function to be passed into a form field ( i.e useField ). Ask questions, find answers and collaborate at work with Stack Overflow for Teams.Explore Teams\n\n##### Collectives™ on Stack Overflow\n\nFind centralized, trusted content and collaborate around the technologies you use most.\n\n Learn more about Collectives \n\n**Teams**\n\nQ\u0026A for work\n\nConnect and share knowledge within a single location that is structured and easy to search.\n\n Learn more about Teams \n\n# How do I use an env file with GitHub Actions?\n\n Ask Question \n\nAsked 5 years, 2 months ago \n\nModified 12 months ago \n\nViewed 180k times\n\n Part of CI/CD Collective\n\n142 \n\nI have multiple environments (dev, qa, prod) and I'm using .env files to store secrets etc... Now I'm switching to GitHub Actions, and I want to use my .env files and declare them into the &#96;env&#96; section of the github actions yml.\n\nBut from what I've seen so far, it seems that I can not set a file path and I have to manually re-declare all variables.\n\nHow should I proceed as best practice?\n\n* github\n* environment-variables\n* github-actions\n\nShare \n\nImprove this question \n\n Follow \n\nedited Apr 8, 2021 at 13:14 \n\nHRK44 \n\n asked Feb 11, 2020 at 19:26 \n\nHRK44's user avatar \n\nHRK44HRK44 \n\n2,78233 gold badges1414 silver badges3333 bronze badges \n\n3 \n\n* 3  \nHi OP! Any luck on this? I'm facing the same issue with Github Actions as well -- trying to figure out a way to somehow store secret variables by different environments.  \n– Vic  \nCommented May 22, 2020 at 2:29\n* 1  \nBasically you have to manually copy the content of the respective .env files (say &#96;.env.stage&#96;, &#96;.env.production&#96;) into the respective GitHub Actions secret variables (say &#96;WEBSITE_ENV_STAGE&#96;, &#96;WEBSITE_ENV_PRODUCTION&#96;). Then at your GitHub Actions workflow script create the &#96;.env&#96; file from the desired variable like this &#96;echo \"${{ secrets.WEBSITE_ENV_STAGE }}\" \u003e .env&#96; and use it in the workflow.  \n– Valentine Shi  \nCommented May 15, 2021 at 3:40\n* I have 2 more ways for you to use &#96;.env&#96; files in your project. See my answer below.  \n– Valentine Shi  \nCommented May 15, 2021 at 4:43\n\nAdd a comment  | \n\n##  16 Answers16 \n\n Sorted by:  Reset to default \n\n Highest score (default)  Trending (recent votes count more)  Date modified (newest first)  Date created (oldest first) \n\n238 \n\nA quick solution here could be having a step to manually create the &#96;.env&#96; file before you need it.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n      - name: 'Create env file'\n        run: |\n          touch .env\n          echo API_ENDPOINT=\"https://xxx.execute-api.us-west-2.amazonaws.com\" \u003e\u003e .env\n          echo API_KEY=${{ secrets.API_KEY }} \u003e\u003e .env\n          cat .env\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nShare \n\nImprove this answer \n\n Follow \n\nedited Feb 14, 2024 at 0:47 \n\n answered Aug 11, 2020 at 1:13 \n\nsugarcane's user avatar \n\nsugarcanesugarcane \n\n2,75011 gold badge1515 silver badges2222 bronze badges \n\n12 \n\n* 18  \nWe have the same solution but this is cumbersome, I have 36 env variables to edit.  \n– aRtoo  \nCommented Aug 26, 2021 at 4:04\n* 1  \nHad to remove the extra \u003e for it to work  \n– wamae  \nCommented Sep 24, 2021 at 12:57\n* 8  \n@aRtoo You can paste your entire env file in one secret named &#96;ENV_FILE&#96; and the just do &#96;echo \"${{ secrets.ENV_FILE }}\" \u003e .env&#96;. I updated the answer with a slightly better approach  \n– DollarAkshay  \nCommented Nov 20, 2022 at 18:46\n* 6  \nCaution: **Never use structured data as a secret**. Structured data can cause secret redaction within logs to fail, because redaction largely relies on finding an exact match for the specific secret value. For example, do not use a blob of JSON, XML, or YAML (or similar) to encapsulate a secret value, as this significantly reduces the probability the secrets will be properly redacted. Instead, create individual secrets for each sensitive value. ref: docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/…  \n– The Fool  \nCommented Jun 10, 2023 at 19:53\n* 2  \n@DollarAkshay you shouldn't be adding your own content when you edit, but rather updating the language for clarity. Your addition belongs in another answer entirely.  \n– dpurrington  \nCommented Oct 27, 2023 at 18:35\n\n | Show **7** more comments \n\n43 \n\nI would suggest 3 pretty simple ways to engage your &#96;.env&#96; file variables in the GitHub Actions workflow. They differ based on whether you store the file in your repository (the worst practice) or keep it out of it (the best practice).\n\n1. You keep your &#96;.env&#96; file in the repository:  \n   * There are some ready-made actions that allow to read the &#96;.env&#96; variables (e.g. Dotenv Action,Simple Dotenv).\n2. (_simple, manual, annoying when update &#96;.env&#96; variables_) You keep your file out of your repository (keep there and maintain updated &#96;.env.example&#96; instead):  \n   * You manually copy the content of the respective &#96;.env&#96; files (say &#96;.env.stage&#96;, &#96;.env.production&#96;) into the respective GitHub Actions secret variables (say &#96;WEBSITE_ENV_STAGE&#96;, &#96;WEBSITE_ENV_PRODUCTION&#96;).  \n   * Then at your GitHub Actions workflow script create the &#96;.env&#96; file from the desired variable like this &#96;echo \"${{secrets.WEBSITE_ENV_STAGE }}\" \u003e .env&#96; and use it in the workflow.\n3. (_a bit more involved though prepare it once, then change your &#96;.env&#96; variables at the local machine, then sync these at GitHub with one click_) As in item 2 above, the file is out of the repository.  \n   * Now you use the GitHub Actions API to create or update the secrets. On your local machine in the &#96;dev&#96; environment you write the NodeJS script that calls the API endpoint and write the &#96;.env&#96; files to the desired GitHub Actions secret variable (say as above into &#96;WEBSITE_ENV_STAGE&#96; or to both stage and production variables at once);\n\nThis is pretty wide choice of ways to engage the &#96;.env&#96; files's variables in the workflow. Use any matching your preference and circumstances.\n\nJust for information, there is the 4th way which engages some 3rd party services like Dotenv Vault or HasiCorp Vault (there are more of the kind) where you keep you secret variables to read these to create &#96;.env&#96; file at build time with your CI/CD pipeline. This question already has quite a few answers—including one that has been extensively validated by the community. Are you certain your approach hasn’t been given previously? **If so, it would be useful to explain how your approach is different, under what circumstances your approach might be preferred, and/or why you think the previous answers aren’t sufficient.** Can you kindly edit your answer to offer an explanation?  \n– Jeremy Caney  \nCommented Sep 23, 2023 at 1:31\n\nAdd a comment  | \n\n4 \n\nThe most modern alternative is to use a &#96;.env.vault&#96; file.\n\nHere's a NodeJS Guide on how to use a .env.vault file with GitHub Actions\n\nIt boils down to 3 steps:\n\n1. Build your encrypted &#96;.env.vault&#96; file and commit that safely to code. This contains an encrypted copy of your CI secrets.\n2. Set a single &#96;DOTENV_KEY&#96; environment variable on GitHub Actions\n3. When the CI runs it will use the &#96;DOTENV_KEY&#96; to decrypt the contents of your &#96;.env.vault&#96; and inject your environment variables just in time.\n\nThis approach is a little more work to initially set up (familiarizing yourself with the new .env.vault file format), but then it has the following benefits:\n\n* No more scattering your secrets across multiple third parties like GitHub Actions that could leak them someday (like what happened with CircleCi breach)\n* You can manage and check your secrets from one central place (rather than having to check GitHub Actions UI to see the value of a secret)\n* If you move CIs everything still just works. You just have to set again that single &#96;DOTENV_KEY&#96;, not a hundred others on the ci server. All your secrets and config are still encrypted inside your &#96;.env.vault&#96; file which lives safely in your repository.\n* An attacker needs access to both your &#96;DOTENV_KEY&#96; and your &#96;.env.vault&#96; file to gain access to your secrets/config. So if GitHub Actions ever has a leak of their CI secrets, your secrets will still be safe because the attacker will only have your &#96;DOTENV_KEY&#96; and not your &#96;.env.vault&#96; file. This will save you the time and annoyance of having to rotate all your secrets.\n\nHope this is useful. Full disclosure: I am the pioneer of dotenv and also run the Dotenv.org service. That said, the mechanism to generate your &#96;.env.vault&#96; file is completely open, local, and free. It's just a file format that uses AES-256 GCM encryption. I wanted the same (or close to) elegance of a .env file but with added security for production and ci deployments. See here for how to use the local only commands or use dotenv.org for the hosted solution.\n\nShare \n\nImprove this answer \n\n Follow \n\n answered Oct 27, 2023 at 17:27 \n\nmot's user avatar \n\nmotmot \n\n12611 silver badge77 bronze badges \n\n1 \n\n* Update: we've moved from &#96;.env.vault&#96; files (which were a bit unwieldy) to inline encrypted &#96;.env*&#96; files. github.com/dotenvx/dotenvx?tab=readme-ov-file#encryption sorry for the change! sometimes progress comes with some missteps.  \n– mot  \nCommented May 16, 2024 at 6:19\n\nAdd a comment  | \n\n3 \n\nI tried using the accepted solution but GitHub actions were complaining about the shell commands. Check it out here: \u003chttps://github.com/zdeneklapes/dotenv-vault-action\u003e.\n\nIt can download the .env file of your choice and will delete all downloaded .env files as a Post Job (after all jobs are completed)!\n\nYou still need to set at least 1 secret, it is your &#96;DOTENV_ME&#96;.\n\n## How to load &#96;.env&#96; variables into the environment?\n\nWhen the &#96;.env&#96; file is downloaded don't forget to load your environment variables using the command &#96;source .env&#96;.\n\n#### Example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n- uses: zdeneklapes/dotenv-vault-action@v1\n        with:\n          dotenvMe: ${{ secrets.DOTENV_ME }}\n          stage: \"ci\"\n          move: \"false\"\n- run: |\n    source .env.ci\n    ssh \"${SSH_USER}@${SSH_HOST}\" \"\n    cd ${DIR_SSH_PROJECT_PRODUCTION} || exit\n    docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml up --build\n    cd - || exit\n    \"\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nShare \n\nImprove this answer \n\n Follow \n\nedited Mar 11, 2024 at 16:23 \n\n answered Mar 11, 2024 at 16:13 \n\nzdeneklapes's user avatar \n\nzdeneklapeszdeneklapes \n\n7511 silver badge66 bronze badges \n\nAdd a comment  | \n\n0 \n\nI was having the same issue. Added &#96;clean: false&#96; under &#96;with&#96; key in my &#96;actions/checkout@v2&#96; in my workflow\n\neg:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\njobs:\n  build:\n\n    runs-on: self-hosted\n\n    strategy:\n      matrix:\n        node-version: [14.x]\n       \n    - uses: actions/checkout@v2\n      with: \n        clean: 'false'\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis prevents git from deleting untracked files like .env.  \n- name: 'Update env file for prod'  \n  run: |  \n    sed -i 's|APP_URL=http://localhost|APP_URL=${{ secrets.APP_URL }}|' .env  \n    sed -i 's|APP_ENVIROMENT=local/APP_ENVIROMENT=${{ secrets.APP_ENVIROMENT }}|' .env  \n    sed -i 's|APP_DEBUG=true/APP_DEBUG=${{ secrets.APP_DEBUG }}|' .env  \n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nNOTE: The Linux sed command for editing an .env file has not been tested.                                                                           |                     |                  |\n\n## Repository files navigation\n\n* README\n* Code of conduct\n* MIT license\n  \n  \nVue Starport \n\nShared Vue component across routes with animations\n\nNPM version\n\nLive Demo\n\nEnglish | 简体中文\n  \n  \n\u003e **Note**: With the View Transitions API coming to the browsers, you may not this library anymore (even tho it's not a 1:1 replacement as View Transition does not preseve dom and state).\n\n## Why?\n\nIt's quite common you might have a same component used in different routes (pages) with a bit different sizes and positions. Sometimes you might want to animate them when user navigates between routes to provide a smooth UX. While such animation is common to be seen in native apps, it's could be a bit challenging to do it in Web.\n\nVue's component structure is presented as a **tree**, and the child components are in different branches with their own instances. Meaning when users navigate between routes, the components are not shared across routes.\n\nBy that means you can't directly animate the changes because they are in two different instances. The good news is, there is a technique called FLIP to enumerate the transitions between them.\n\nHowever, FLIP only solves the problem of transitions, the components are still not the same. During the navigation, the internal state of the component will lost.\n\nThus I started this new approach **Starport** to experiment with a better solution to fit this requirement.\n\n## How?\n\nSo since we can't share the components across different branches in the component tree, we could actually hoist them to the root so they become independent from the routes.\n\nTo allow each page to still have control of the components, we introduced a **Proxy component** to present the expected size and position of that component. The proxy will pass the props and position information to the actual component and let it \"fly over\" the proxy with animations.\n\nWhen the transition ends and it arrived to the expected position, it will then \"land down\" to the actual component using the \u003cTeleport/\u003e component.\n\nWith this \"landing\" mechanism, the DOM tree will be preserved as what you will have with the original tree structure. When navigating to another route, the component then will \"lift off\" back to the floating state, \"fly\" to the new proxy's position and \"land\" again.\n\nThis is very similar to Terran's Buildings in StarCraft (able to leave the ground and fly to new locations). It's also the inspiration source of the project name **Starport**.\n\n## Install\n\n\u003e ⚗️ **Experimental**\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm i vue-starport\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n\u003e Vue Starport only works for Vue 3\n\n## Usage\n\nAdd &#96;\u003cStarportCarrier\u003e&#96; component from &#96;vue-starport&#96; to your root component (&#96;app.vue&#96;). All &#96;\u003cStarport\u003e&#96; usage should be inside &#96;\u003cStarportCarrier\u003e&#96; component.\n\n\u003cscript setup\u003e\nimport { StarportCarrier } from 'vue-starport'\n\u003c/script\u003e\n\n\u003ctemplate\u003e\n  \u003cStarportCarrier\u003e \u003c!-- here --\u003e\n    \u003cRouterView /\u003e\n  \u003c/StarportCarrier\u003e\n\u003c/template\u003e\n\nIn routes, wrap the component with the &#96;\u003cStarport\u003e&#96; component.\n\n\u003c!-- PageA.vue --\u003e\n\u003cscript setup\u003e\nimport { Starport } from 'vue-starport'\n\u003c/script\u003e\n\n\u003ctemplate\u003e\n  \u003cdiv\u003e\n    \u003c!-- ... --\u003e\n    \u003cStarport port=\"my-id\" style=\"height:400px\"\u003e \n      \u003cMyComponent :prop=\"value\"/\u003e\n    \u003c/Starport\u003e\n  \u003c/div\u003e\n\u003c/template\u003e\n\nOn the other page, we do the same thing with **the same &#96;port&#96; id** to identify the instance.\n\n\u003c!-- PageB.vue --\u003e\n\u003cscript setup\u003e\nimport { Starport } from 'vue-starport'\n\u003c/script\u003e\n\n\u003ctemplate\u003e\n  \u003cdiv\u003e\n    \u003c!-- ... --\u003e\n    \u003cStarport port=\"my-id\" style=\"height:600px\"\u003e\n      \u003cMyComponent :prop=\"value\"/\u003e\n    \u003c/Starport\u003e\n  \u003c/div\u003e\n\u003c/template\u003e\n\n\u003e Note that you might need to apply some styles to &#96;\u003cStarport\u003e&#96; to make it have a defined size indicating the area for the \"floating starcraft\" to land.\n\nCheckout the Playground for more examples.\n\n### Register Components Globally\n\n// main.ts\nimport StarportPlugin from 'vue-starport'\n\napp.use(StarportPlugin())\n\nAnd then you can use &#96;Starport&#96; and &#96;StarportCarrier&#96; components without importing.\n\n### Keep Alive\n\nBy default, when navigating to a page without a corresponding &#96;\u003cStarport\u003e&#96; proxy to land, the component will be destroyed. If you want to keep the component alive even when it's not presented in the current route, you can set &#96;keepAlive&#96; to &#96;true&#96; for that specific instance.\n\n\u003cStarport keep-alive port=\"my-id\"\u003e\n  \u003cMyComponent /\u003e\n\u003c/Starport\u003e\n\nTo configure it globally, you can pass options to the plugin:\n\n// main.ts\nimport StarportPlugin from 'vue-starport'\n\napp.use(StarportPlugin({ keepAlive: true }))\n\n## Debug\n\nTo debug what happens during the transition, you can add the follow CSS to highlight the parts\n\n[data-starport-craft] {\n  background: #0805;\n}\n[data-starport-proxy]:not([data-starport-landed]) {\n  background: #8005;\n}\n\n## Special Thanks\n\nThanks to @hangsman who helped to provide the initial solution of proper teleport the element and made this idea valid. Also thanks to the viewers of my live-streaming on Bilibili, those who spend time with me to working on this idea and provided useful feedback during the live.\n\nYou can check the recordings of my live-streams (in Chinese), where I wrote this project from scratch.\n\n你可以在哔哩哔哩观看我实现此项目的 直播录像。\n\n## Sponsors\n\n## License\n\nMIT License © 2022 Anthony Fu\n\n## About\n\n 🛰 Shared component across routes with animations\n\nvue-starport.netlify.app/ \n\n### Resources\n\n Readme \n\n### License\n\n MIT license \n\n### Code of conduct\n\n Code of conduct \n\nActivity \n\n### Stars\n\n**1.9k** stars \n\n### Watchers\n\n**8** watching \n\n### Forks\n\n**98** forks \n\n Report repository \n\n## Releases2\n\nv0.4.0  Latest Sep 7, 2023 \n\n\\+ 1 release\n\n## Sponsor this project\n\n Sponsor \n\nLearn more about GitHub Sponsors \n\n## Contributors13\n\n## Languages\n\n* TypeScript 67.1%\n* Vue 23.8%\n* JavaScript 5.4%\n* HTML 2.1%\n* CSS 1.6%\n\n## Footer\n\n © 2025 GitHub, Inc. \n\n### Footer navigation\n\n* Terms\n* Privacy\n* Security\n* Status\n* Docs\n* Contact\n* Manage cookies\n* Do not share my personal information\n\n You can’t perform that action at this time.",

                                                                     |                                                                                                                |                     |                  |\n\n## Repository files navigation\n\n* README\n* Code of conduct\n* MIT-0 license\n* Security\n\n# cloudscape-form-builder Readme\n\nThis solution was built to accelerate the development of web forms on the frontend using the AWS Cloudscape Design System. Cloudscape is an open source design system to create web applications. It was built for and is used by Amazon Web Services (AWS) products and services. We created it in 2016 to improve the user experience across web applications owned by AWS services, and also to help teams implement those applications faster. Since then, we have continued enhancing the system based on customer feedback and research.\n\nThis solution provides you with a sample application that utilises components of the Cloudscape Design System that are commonly used in web-forms where users are required to input data. A &#96;FormBuilder&#96; component is included that can be imported into your own application to help you rapidly develop your own forms for your Cloudscape based web application. Many of the form based components are pre-configured to ensure that you can quickly build forms for many different use cases. These forms are defined in templates within &#96;src/forms/form-configs.ts&#96; and passed to the &#96;FormBuilder&#96; component. The &#96;FormBuilder&#96; and &#96;FormElement&#96; components take care of the heavy lifting to render both read-only and editable forms where ever you need them in your application. This takes alot of the work out of building forms, by managing form state, submission and change functions and also takes care of the UI layout for you.\n\nThe solution has been designed with experimentation in mind. It includes a 'Form Playground' that you can use to preview your form configurations, before porting the provided components to your own application. You can also use this solution as a scaffolded application to kickstart your own frontend project built on the AWS Cloudscape Design System\n\n## Requirements\n\n* nodejs \\- version 18 or later.\n* TypeScript \\- via npm\n* Vite\n* React\n\n## Getting Started\n\n1. Create a new directory, navigate to that directory in a terminal and clone the GitHub repository:  \n&#96;&#96;&#96;  \ngit clone https://github.com/aws-samples/webapp-form-builder  \n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n2. Change directory to the pattern directory:  \n&#96;&#96;&#96;  \ncd webapp-form-builder  \n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n3. You should end up with a working directory that looks like this. The structure is explained below.  \n├── README.md  \n├── index.html  \n├── package-lock.json  \n├── package.json  \n├── src  \n│   ├── App.tsx  \n│   ├── components  \n│   │   ├── Breadcrumbs.tsx  \n│   │   ├── HelpPanelContent.tsx  \n│   │   ├── Navigation.tsx  \n│   │   ├── TopNavigation.tsx  \n│   │   └── customHelpPanels.tsx  \n│   ├── forms  \n│   │   ├── FormBuilder.tsx  \n│   │   ├── FormElement.tsx  \n│   │   ├── Forms.ts  \n│   │   ├── components  \n│   │   │   ├── BannerAlert.tsx  \n│   │   │   ├── DatePicker.tsx  \n│   │   │   ├── InputField.tsx  \n│   │   │   ├── InputFieldWithRadio.tsx  \n│   │   │   ├── InputTextArea.tsx  \n│   │   │   ├── MultiSelectField.tsx  \n│   │   │   ├── SelectField.tsx  \n│   │   │   ├── TilesSelect.tsx  \n│   │   │   └── TilesWithSelect.tsx  \n│   │   └── form-configs.ts  \n│   ├── helpers  \n│   │   └── UseLink.ts  \n│   ├── main.tsx  \n│   ├── pages  \n│   │   ├── error  \n│   │   │   ├── Error.tsx  \n│   │   │   └── components  \n│   │   │       └── ErrorContent.tsx  \n│   │   ├── form  \n│   │   │   ├── Form.tsx  \n│   │   │   └── components  \n│   │   │       └── FormContent.tsx  \n│   │   └── home  \n│   │       ├── Home.tsx  \n│   │       └── components  \n│   │           └── HomeContent.tsx  \n│   └── vite-env.d.ts  \n├── tsconfig.app.json  \n├── tsconfig.json  \n├── tsconfig.node.json  \n└── vite.config.ts\n4. Run the solution locally  \n&#96;&#96;&#96;  \nnpm install \u0026\u0026 npm run dev  \n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n5. Launch the application in a browser  \n&#96;&#96;&#96;  \nhttp://localhost:5173/  \n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n6. Open your IDE, we are ready to start building some forms.\n\n## How does it work?\n\n### First, lets walk through the project file structure:\n\n└── src\n    ├── components\n    ├── forms\n    │   ├── FormBuilder.tsx\n    │   ├── FormElement.tsx\n    │   ├── Forms.ts\n    │   ├── components\n    │   └── form-configs.ts\n    ├── helpers\n    └── pages\n        ├── error\n        ├── form\n        └── home\n\n* &#96;components&#96; \\- This contains are global components that are used throughout the solution\n* &#96;forms&#96; \\- This is where the &#96;FormBuilder&#96; and &#96;FormElement&#96; components live.\n* &#96;forms/components&#96; \\- This is where we master components that are used by the &#96;FormBuilder&#96; and &#96;FormElement&#96; components. You can add your own form components to this directory to be used by the &#96;FormBuilder&#96; and &#96;FormElement&#96; components\n* &#96;helpers&#96; \\- contains helper functions that are used throughout the solution\n* &#96;pages&#96; \\- contains the heirarchy of pages that are rendered throughout the solution. Usually when you want to display a form, you will render it to a page. You can create your own page following the layout in this directory. Start by cloning an exisitng page and updating it with your values. You will need to import the page into the &#96;router&#96; in &#96;src/main.tsx&#96;\n* &#96;pages/form&#96; \\- This is the 'Form Playground' page - You can update this form to experment by modifying the template in &#96;src/forms/form-configs.ts&#96;\n\n### How do I build my own form?\n\nTo quickly get started, navigate to &#96;src/forms/form-configs.ts&#96; \\- You will see an &#96;exampleForm&#96; that is displayed within the 'Form Playground.' You can edit this to see it displayed **immediately** in the UI.\n\nexport const exampleForm: FormConfigItem[] = [\n  {\n    inputType: \"SELECT\",\n    name: \"timeOfDay\",\n    containerName: \"Select - containerName\",\n    description: \"description - This is a 'SELECT' example\",\n    label: \"Example - label\",\n    options: selectOptions,\n  },\n  {\n    inputType: \"INPUT\",\n    type: \"text\",\n    name: \"firstName\",\n    containerName: \"First Name\",\n    description: \"This is a 'INPUT' example\",\n    label: \"Label\",\n    helpPanelIndex: 0,\n  },\n  ...\n]\n\nForms are built from different types of input components. Within this solution, you can find useable input components defined in &#96;src/forms/Forms.ts&#96;\n\nexport type FormConfigItem = {\n  name: string;\n  containerName: string;\n  helpPanelIndex?: number;\n  description: string;\n  label: string;\n} \u0026 (\n  | {\n      inputType: \"TILES\";\n      options: Option[];\n    }\n  | {\n      inputType: \"TILES_WITH_SELECT\";\n      options: Option[];\n      secondName: string;\n      secondLabel: string;\n      secondOptions: Option[];\n    }\n  | {\n      inputType: \"SELECT\";\n      options: Option[];\n    }\n  | {\n      inputType: \"INPUT_WITH_RADIO\";\n      type: \"text\";\n      secondName: string;\n      secondLabel: string;\n      options: Option[];\n    }\n  | {\n      inputType: \"INPUT\";\n      type: \"text\";\n    }\n  | {\n      inputType: \"TEXTAREA\";\n      helpPanelIndex: number;\n    }\n  | {\n      inputType: \"MULTISELECT\";\n      options: Option[];\n    }\n  | {\n      inputType: \"DATE_PICKER\";\n    }\n);\n\nHere you can see that all components defined for usage in our form template require the following **common** properties:\n\n* &#96;name&#96; \\- &#96;string&#96; \\- Name is the input field name for the generated payload - this is not displayed in the UI\n* &#96;containerName&#96; \\- &#96;string&#96; \\- The container heading that is displayed in the UI\n* &#96;description&#96; \\- &#96;string&#96; \\- The string description that will be displayed under the container label - use an empty string (&#96;\"\"&#96;) if you dont want to display this.\n* &#96;label&#96; \\- &#96;string&#96; \\- The container label\n* &#96;inputType&#96; \\- &#96;INPUT&#96; or &#96;TEXTAREA&#96; or &#96;DATE_PICKER&#96; etc (as shown in &#96;FormConfigItem&#96; above)\n\nSome input components require **additional** properties, especially when using a selectable component, like &#96;MULTISELECT&#96;. This also requires an &#96;options&#96; prop, of type &#96;array&#96;. Two examples have been provided (shown below) in &#96;form-configs.ts&#96;\n\n// Sample Form Options\nexport const selectOptions = [\n  { label: \"Morning\", value: \"morning\" },\n  { label: \"Afternoon\", value: \"afternoon\" },\n  { label: \"Evening\", value: \"evening\" },\n  { label: \"Night\", value: \"night\" },\n]\n\nexport const multiSelectOptions = [\n  { label: \"Red\", value: \"red\", description: \"A red option\" },\n  { label: \"Blue\", value: \"blue\", description: \"A blue option\" },\n  { label: \"Green\", value: \"green\", description: \"A green option\" },\n  { label: \"Yellow\", value: \"yellow\", description: \"A yellow option\" },\n  { label: \"Purple\", value: \"purple\", description: \"A purple option\" },\n  { label: \"Orange\", value: \"orange\", description: \"An orange option\" },\n  { label: \"Pink\", value: \"pink\", description: \"A pink option\" },\n  { label: \"Brown\", value: \"brown\", description: \"A brown option\" },\n  { label: \"Black\", value: \"black\", description: \"A black option\" },\n]\n\nYou can build your own multi-select options by following this pattern, or fetching these from your database. You will need to be aware of the input props required by each component type to render data - you can find the documentation for Multiselect here. Follow this approach for each different type of component you choose to use.\n\nHere is an example of defining a form to collect a users first and last name. Pass this to the &#96;FormElement&#96; and &#96;FormBuilder&#96; to render it on the page.\n\nexport const basicForm: FormConfigItem[] = [\n  {\n    inputType: \"INPUT\",\n    type: \"text\",\n    name: \"firstName\",\n    containerName: \"First Name\",\n    description: \"Enter your first name\",\n    label: \"Label\",\n  },\n  {\n    inputType: \"INPUT\",\n    type: \"text\",\n    name: \"surname\",\n    containerName: \"Surname\",\n    description: \"Enter your surname\",\n    label: \"Detail Label\",\n  },\n]; \n\n### What if I want to use a component that is not included?\n\nYou can add your own components to be used within the &#96;FormElement&#96; and &#96;FormBuilder&#96;. Lets walk through the process below:\n\n1. Find the component you want to use from the Cloudscape Design System component library \\- For this example we will use Date input\n2. Define the component in &#96;src/forms/components&#96; by creating &#96;DateInput.tsx&#96;  \n // UI  \n import Container from \"@cloudscape-design/components/container\";  \n import Header from \"@cloudscape-design/components/header\";  \n import DateInput from \"@cloudscape-design/components/date-input\";  \n import FormField from \"@cloudscape-design/components/form-field\";  \n import { FieldProps } from \"../Forms\";  \n type InputFieldProps = FieldProps \u0026 {};  \n const DateInputField = ({  \n   label,  \n   value,  \n   onChange,  \n   readOnly,  \n   description,  \n   containerName,  \n }: InputFieldProps) =\u003e {  \n   return (  \n     \u003cContainer header={\u003cHeader variant=\"h2\"\u003e{containerName}\u003c/Header\u003e}\u003e  \n       \u003cFormField label={label} description={description}\u003e  \n         \u003cDateInput  \n           onChange={({ detail }) =\u003e onChange(detail.value)}  \n           value={value}  \n           disabled={readOnly}  \n           placeholder=\"YYYY/MM/DD\"  \n         /\u003e  \n       \u003c/FormField\u003e  \n     \u003c/Container\u003e  \n   );  \n };  \n export default DateInputField;\n3. Update &#96;FormConfigItem&#96; in &#96;src/forms/Forms.ts&#96; to include the new &#96;inputType&#96; for the component we just created.  \n export type FormConfigItem = {  \n name: string;  \n containerName: string;  \n helpPanelIndex?: number;  \n description: string;  \n label: string;  \n } \u0026 (  \n   | {  \n     inputType: \"DATE_INPUT\";  \n   }  \n   ...  \n )\n4. In &#96;src/forms/FormBuilder.tsx&#96; import the new component - &#96;DateInputField&#96; in this example - &#96;import DateInputField from \"./components/DateInput\";&#96;\n5. In &#96;src/forms/FormBuilder.tsx&#96; update the &#96;renderField&#96; function to include another case statement. The &#96;FormBuilder&#96; will iterate through a form templates &#96;inputType&#96; property to work out what component to render to the UI.  \n case \"DATE_INPUT\":  \n return \u003cDateInputField {...commonProps} {...field} /\u003e;\n6. Update your form template to use the new component  \n export const basicForm: FormConfigItem[] = [  \n   {  \n     inputType: \"INPUT\",  \n     type: \"text\",  \n     name: \"firstName\",  \n     containerName: \"First Name\",  \n     description: \"Enter your first name\",  \n     label: \"Label\",  \n   },  \n   {  \n     inputType: \"INPUT\",  \n     type: \"text\",  \n     name: \"surname\",  \n     containerName: \"Surname\",  \n     description: \"Enter your surname\",  \n     label: \"Detail Label\",  \n   },  \n   {  \n     inputType: \"DATE_INPUT\",  \n     name: \"birthday\",  \n     containerName: \"Date Input\",  \n     description: \"Enter your birthday\",  \n     label: \"Example Label\",  \n   },  \n ];\n7. Review the 'Form Playground' page to see the component rendered in the UIexample form\n\n### Why are there two different components that I can use?\n\nThere are indeed two different components implemented and used throughout this solution:\n\n* &#96;FormBuilder&#96;\n* &#96;FormElement&#96;\n\nThe focus of this solution is around a \"Form Builder\" for the AWS Cloudscape Design System, but the &#96;FormBuilder&#96; component can be used in two different scenarios:\n\n* In isolation, to render read-only components for displaying data in a view or page.\n* In a HTML &#96;form&#96; element to capture input data for the backend. If you need to build a form, use the &#96;FormElement&#96; component. This will import and use the &#96;FormBuilder&#96; for you, whilst providing benefits of a HTML &#96;form&#96; element\n\nThis solution utilises both approaches to provide you with \"editable\" forms, and includes appropraite react state management to switch the form between \"edit mode\" and \"read-only.\" You can toggle the state with the \"Edit\" button found in the top right corner of the \"Form Playground\" page\n\n### Can I use the FormBuilder and FormELement components in my own application?\n\nOf course! This will require some knowledge of react to port/migrate these components to your own application, but it is absolutely do-able. Start off by moving the &#96;src/forms&#96; folder to your app. Then you can import components and utilise them as needed.\n\n## Security\n\nSee CONTRIBUTING for more information.\n\n## License\n\nThis library is licensed under the MIT-0 License. See the LICENSE file.\n\n## About\n\n This solution was built to accelerate the development of web forms on the frontend using the AWS Cloudscape Design System. Cloudscape is an open source design system to create web applications. It was built for and is used by Amazon Web Services (AWS) products and services.\n\n### Resources\n\n Readme \n\n### License\n\n MIT-0 license \n\n### Code of conduct\n\n Code of conduct \n\n### Security policy\n\n Security policy \n\nActivity \n\nCustom properties \n\n### Stars\n\n**16** stars \n\n### Watchers\n\n**2** watching \n\n### Forks\n\n**1** fork \n\n Report repository \n\n## Contributors2\n\n## Languages\n\n* TypeScript 97.6%\n* JavaScript 1.3%\n* HTML 1.1%\n\n## Footer\n\n © 2025 GitHub, Inc. \n\n### Footer navigation\n\n* Terms\n* Privacy\n* Security\n* Status\n* Docs\n* Contact\n* Manage cookies\n* Do not share my personal information\n\n You can’t perform that action at this time.",

Repository files navigation\n\n* README\n* MIT license\n\n# Next JS Gravity Forms Component\n\nA plug and play component for parsing GraphQL Gravity Form data. Outputs a component using BEM classes, meaning all you need to do is style it.\n\nTo be used alongside wp-graphql-gravity-forms (version 0.12.0 up).\n\nUses React Hook Forms under the hood for all that good state management.\n\n## Installation\n\neither:\n\n### Install with yarn\n\nyarn add next-gravity-forms\n\nor\n\n### Install with NPM\n\nnpm i next-gravity-forms\n\n## How To Use\n\nAdd the env variable to your project: &#96;NEXT_PUBLIC_WORDPRESS_API_URL&#96;. Add your domain to it. i.e.&#96;NEXT_PUBLIC_WORDPRESS_API_URL=https://www.YOURWPSITE.com/graphql&#96;.\n\nThis variable is called internally by the &#96;getGravityForm&#96; function.\n\nImport the component and use it with the API function. Select the required form using its &#96;databaseId&#96;.\n\nimport GravityFormForm from \"next-gravity-forms\";\nimport { getGravityForm } from \"next-gravity-forms/server\";\n\nconst data = await getGravityForm(1);\n\nreturn \u003cGravityFormForm data={data} /\u003e;\n\n### Redirecting\n\nThis package can be used with any React project. We just named it Next, because we use it with Next projects.\n\nTo allow it to be flexible, we have added a number of arguments to the main component.\n\nconst GravityFormForm = ({\n  data,\n  presetValues = () =\u003e {},\n  successCallback = () =\u003e {},\n  errorCallback = {},\n  navigate,\n  helperText = {}\n  customFormFields = {}\n})\n\n* data: The form data needed to create the form. Got via &#96;getGravityForm&#96; query.\n* presetValues: Any preset values needed to pass in - see below.\n* successCallback: Function that is called when form is successul.\n* errorCallback: Function that is called when the form errors.\n* navigate: Function that is called with URL for redirecting the user.\n* helperText: Object with values to override strings - see the Translation section.\n* customFormFields: Object that allows you to override form fields. See the Custom Form Fields section.\n\n### Caching\n\nIf you are wanting to use a provider like Stellate to cache your form queries, pass the Stellate URL to &#96;NEXT_PUBLIC_WORDPRESS_API_URL&#96;.\n\nYou will then need to pass in a clean URL for the form to submit. This can be passed in with &#96;NEXT_PUBLIC_WORDPRESS_FORM_SUBMIT_URL&#96;.\n\nNote: If &#96;NEXT_PUBLIC_WORDPRESS_FORM_SUBMIT_URL&#96; is not passed in, it will fall back to &#96;NEXT_PUBLIC_WORDPRESS_API_URL&#96;.\n\n### Passing in Preset Values\n\nSometimes you will want to conditionally set default values, or pass in data to hidden fields. This could be values for a user ID, or a current page.\n\nThis is handled by the &#96;presetValues&#96; prop. In addition, you need to pass your query parameters within this prop to make dynamically populating field work. Good to know that the query string takes priority over the field name parameter.\n\n\u003cGravityFormForm\n  data={form}\n  presetValues={{ ...queryParams, input_2: \"My preset value\" }}\n/\u003e\n\nIn the above example &#96;input_2&#96; corresponds to the 2nd field added in the WordPress Gravity Forms edit page. This value can be found by clicking on the field and looking at the top right just under Field Settings.\n\n### Translation\n\nSince package uses some hardcoded strings, we implemented the way how to translate them to your preferable text.&#96;helperText&#96; prop should be used to override it. You can find all possible strings here. You can handle your own translations by passing in different strings depending on what is needed, and they will be merged with the existing ones. Alternatively, you can pass an entire object with translations for all strings. See the example below:\n\n\u003cGravityFormForm\n  data={form}\n  helperText={{\n    errors: {\n      general: \"There was a problem with your submission. Check errors\",\n      leastOneField: \"At least one field must be filled out.\",\n      required: \"Field is required.\",\n      pattern: {\n        email: \"The email address is invalid\",\n        phone: \"This is an invalid phone\",\n      },\n    },\n    radio: {\n      otherChoice: \"Other\", // alternatively you can override only specific field, .i.e. otherChoice_3\n    },\n  }}\n/\u003e\n\n## WordPress Backend Not Allowing Submission\n\nHaving CORS issues?\n\nAdd the following snippet of code to your WordPress functions.php file.\n\nMake sure to update the '\u003chttps://yourfrontendurl.com\u003e' to your actual frontend. With no trailing slash.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nadd_filter( 'graphql_response_headers_to_send', function( $headers ) {\n\treturn array_merge( $headers, [\n\t\t'Access-Control-Allow-Origin'  =\u003e 'https://yourfrontendurl.com',\n\t\t'Access-Control-Allow-Methods' =\u003e 'POST, GET, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE',\n\t\t'Access-Control-Allow-Credentials' =\u003e 'true'\n\t] );\n} );\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Implementing Google reCAPTCHA\n\nOn your WordPress backend within the Gravity Forms settings set up reCaptcha. Follow the instructions provided by Gravity Forms.\n\n## File Upload\n\nTo enable file uploading functionality, your GraphQL server must support the &#96;Upload&#96; scalar type. In WordPress, this can be easily achieved by installing the WP GraphQL Upload plugin.\n\nIf you attempt to add a file upload field to your form without support for the &#96;Upload&#96; scalar type, your API will return an error. Ensure that your GraphQL server is properly configured to handle file uploads by integrating the WP GraphQL Upload plugin or another equivalent solution that provides support for the &#96;Upload&#96; type.\n\nWhen enabling the &#96;Enable Multi-File Upload&#96; option, it's important to note that files are not uploaded immediately upon being dropped into the upload area. Instead, all files are uploaded together during the form submission process. However, be aware that this can introduce a delay, particularly when users upload large files. Might be good to show spinner while uploading.\n\n## Date field\n\nThe &#96;Date Picker&#96; functionality in our form utilizes the &#96;react-datepicker&#96; package. Please note that this package does not include default styles. To ensure proper styling of the date picker, you must either provide your own custom styles or import the default styles from the package. To use the default styles, include the following import statement in your code:\n\nimport \"react-datepicker/dist/react-datepicker.css\";\n\nAdditionally, our component allows you to customize the settings of the DatePicker through the &#96;helperFieldsSettings&#96; prop. This is particularly useful for setting constraints like the maximum year. For instance, to set the maximum year to &#96;2024&#96;, you would configure the prop as follows:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003cGravityFormForm\n  data={form}\n  helperFieldsSettings={{\n    date: {\n     dateMaxYear: 2024\n    },\n  }}\n/\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nFor a complete list of customizable options for the DatePicker, refer to the fieldsSettings.js file available in our repository: fieldsSettings.js.\n\n## Number field\n\nAs you probably know, the Number field has an option to set the currency format. By default, we support only EUR, USD, and GBP currencies. If you would like to add a custom currency, other than set it by &#96;gform_currency&#96; filter, you also need to pass it as a prop using the &#96;helperFieldsSettings&#96; prop, as follows:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003cGravityFormForm\n  data={form}\n  helperFieldsSettings={{\n    number: {\n     currencies: {\n      HKD: {\n        symbol_left: \"HK$\",\n        symbol_right: \"\",\n        symbol_padding: \"\",\n        thousand_separator: \",\",\n        decimal_separator: \".\",\n        decimals: 2,\n      }\n     }\n    },\n  }}\n/\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Exposed methods\n\nWe expose several &#96;react-hook-form&#96; methods for flexible form management.\n\n* &#96;setError(name, error)&#96; \\- Set an error for a field.\n* &#96;reset()&#96; \\- Reset the form.\n* &#96;getValues(name)&#96; \\- Get the value of a field or all values.\n* &#96;setValue(name, value)&#96; \\- Set the value of a field.\n* &#96;watch(name)&#96; \\- Watch for changes to a field.\n\nconst GravityForm = ({ data }) =\u003e {\n  const formRef = useRef();\n\n  const handleReset = () =\u003e formRef.current.reset();\n  const handleSetValue = () =\u003e\n    formRef.current.setValue(\"exampleField\", \"new value\");\n\n  return (\n    \u003cdiv\u003e\n      \u003cGravityFormForm ref={formRef} data={data} /\u003e\n      \u003cbutton onClick={handleReset}\u003eReset Form\u003c/button\u003e\n      \u003cbutton onClick={handleSetValue}\u003eSet Field Value\u003c/button\u003e\n    \u003c/div\u003e\n  );\n};\n\nexport default GravityForm;\n\n## Custom Form Fields\n\nSometimes you may need to render custom markup for specific fields. You can achieve this by using the &#96;customFormFields&#96; property. See the example below:\n\n\u003cGravityFormForm data={form} customFormFields={{ 1: CustomInputComponent }} /\u003e\n\nBy specifying the field ID that you want to override, you can pass your custom component. Note that your custom component must utilize the methods provided by react-hook-form, as it is registered using the Controller component.\n\nExample of your custom component:\n\nconst CustomInputComponent = ({ value, onChange, onBlur, ...rest }) =\u003e {\n  return (\n    \u003cdiv className=\"example\"\u003e\n      \u003cinput\n        type=\"text\"\n        value={value}\n        onChange={onChange}\n        onBlur={onBlur}\n        {...rest}\n      /\u003e\n    \u003c/div\u003e\n  );\n};\n\nTake into account that your field must return the value in the same format as a default field.\n\n## Testing \u0026 Developing\n\nFirstly, yes please! Any help would be great.\n\n### How to get started\n\nThere are a few steps to get a dev enviroment set up.\n\n* Clone repo\n* Clone \u003chttps://github.com/robmarshall/next-gravity-forms-example\u003e to a different location\n* Remove the next-gravity-forms package from the above example repo package.json\n* Install packages on example repo\n* Navigate into your local \"next-gravity-forms\" root.\n* Install packages\n* Build it using \"yarn build\"\n* Navigate into the /dist folder and run yarn link\n* Navigate back to the example repo root and run yarn link \"next-gravity-forms\"\n\nYou should now be able to run the example repo and see the dev form package running.\n\nCurrently whenever you make a change you will need to re-run &#96;yarn build&#96;. A hot-reload is yet to be added.\n\n## To Do\n\n### Field Components\n\n* Input\n* Textarea\n* Select\n* Multiselect\n* Number\n* Checkbox\n* Radio\n* Hidden\n* HTML\n* Captcha\n* Add masking to inputs\n* Section\n* Page (half done, need to save values so that when the user refreshes the page, they are preserved)\n* Date\n* File upload\n* Post Fields\n* Pricing Fields\n* Phone (doesn't support custom phone type)\n* Email\n* Consent\n* Website\n* Password\n* Configure error message (currently just 'An Unknown Error Occurred')\n* Integrate Success/Failure Handler from previous plugin\n\n### General Form\n\n* Honeypot\n* Save and Continue\n* Add submit/error callback for custom use\n\n### Add Tests to Inputs\n\n* Input\n* Textarea\n* Select (half done, need to add default values)\n* Multiselect\n* Number\n* Checkbox (half done, need to add default values)\n* Radio (half done, need to add default values)\n* Hidden\n* HTML\n* Captcha\n* Consent\n* Website\n* Phone\n* Page\n* Date\n* \\[\\] Password (almost done, test can be tweaked)\n\n## Confirmations\n\n* Text Confirmation (&#96;{all_fields}&#96; is not supported)\n* Page Change\n* Redirect\n* Redirect query strings support only form fields (excluding file uploads) and do not support user/entry-related fields (e.g., User IP, entry ID)\n* Conditional Logic\n\n## Known Issues\n\n* Invalid phone number results in failed submission w/ non-descript general error message.\n* Setting the Submit Button Location to 'End of the Last Row' causes a fetch API error, as GraphQL doesn't support it yet.\n* Password confirmation doesn't work with &#96;wp-graphql-gravity-forms&#96; version &#96;0.13.0.1&#96; and earlier. To fix this, add a copy of the general password value as the &#96;input_2&#96; value in the $\\_POST submission.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## About\n\n No description, website, or topics provided.\n\n### Resources\n\n Readme \n\n### License\n\n MIT license \n\nActivity \n\n### Stars\n\n**7** stars \n\n### Watchers\n\n**2** watching \n\n### Forks\n\n**12** forks \n\n Report repository \n\n## Releases\n\n2 tags \n\n## Packages0\n\n No packages published   \n\n## Contributors9\n\n## Languages\n\n* JavaScript 100.0%\n\n## Footer\n\n © 2025 GitHub, Inc. \n\n### Footer navigation\n\n* Terms\n* Privacy\n* Security\n* Status\n* Docs\n* Contact\n* Manage cookies\n* Do not share my personal information\n\n You can’t perform that action at this time.",

They're just deployment details -- and there are lots of tools to help manage environment variables -- not the least handy being a simple .env file with all your settings. Simply source the appropriate env before you launch the app in the given env (you could make it part of a launch script, for instance).\n\nenv files look like this:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nSOMEVAR=\"somevalue\"\nANOTHERVAR=\"anothervalue\"\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTo source it:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n$ source dev.env  # or staging.env, or production.env, depending on where you're deploying to\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nDon't check these files into the repo... instead, check in something like dev.example.env, containing some sensible defaults, minus your app secrets, of course. Devs wishing to collaborate should copy the file to the real filename, set the values appropriately, and they're off to the races.\n\nIt's easy to add scripts via npm, so you can source the appropriate env file by running commands:\n\nIn your package.json:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nscripts: {\n  \"start-dev\": \"source dev.env; node server.js\"\n  \"start-prod\": \"source prod.env; node server.js\"\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThen start it up:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n$ npm run start-prod\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n@alielzei \n\n Copy link \n\n### \n\n**alielzei**  commented Apr 2, 2017 \n\nyou my friend are a simple genius\n\n Sorry, something went wrong.\n\n@robophil \n\n Copy link \n\n### \n\n**robophil**  commented Apr 20, 2017 \n\n@Alizzen, my thoughts exactly\n\n Sorry, something went wrong.\n\n@JohnnyBizzel \n\n Copy link \n\n### \n\n**JohnnyBizzel**  commented Apr 24, 2017 \n\nI get \"source\" not found. Repository files navigation\n\n* README\n\n# Vue 3 + Typescript + Vite\n\nThis template should help get you started developing with Vue 3 and Typescript in Vite. The template uses Vue 3 &#96;\u003cscript setup\u003e&#96; SFCs, check out the script setup docs to learn more.\n\n## Recommended IDE Setup\n\n* VSCode \\+ Volar\n\n## Type Support For &#96;.vue&#96; Imports in TS\n\nSince TypeScript cannot handle type information for &#96;.vue&#96; imports, they are shimmed to be a generic Vue component type by default. In most cases this is fine if you don't really care about component prop types outside of templates. However, if you wish to get actual prop types in &#96;.vue&#96; imports (for example to get props validation when using manual &#96;h(...)&#96; calls), you can enable Volar's &#96;.vue&#96; type support plugin by running &#96;Volar: Switch TS Plugin on/off&#96; from VSCode command palette.**##author : Mark Teves**\n\n## About\n\nsupabase-form.vercel.app/ \n\n### Resources\n\n Readme \n\nActivity \n\n### Stars\n\n**1** star \n\n### Watchers\n\n**1** watching \n\n### Forks\n\n**0** forks \n\n Report repository \n\n## Releases\n\nNo releases published\n\n## Packages0\n\n No packages published   \n\n## Contributors3\n\n## Languages\n\n* Vue 71.5%\n* TypeScript 21.0%\n* CSS 6.7%\n* HTML 0.8%\n\n## Footer\n\n © 2025 GitHub, Inc. \n\n### Footer navigation\n\n* Terms\n* Privacy\n* Security\n* Status\n* Docs\n* Contact\n* Manage cookies\n* Do not share my personal information\n\n You can’t perform that action at this time.",
